question: Why is it architecturally significant that AI agents are participants rather than a separate system?
options: It means agents automatically inherit every platform capability — encryption, NAT traversal, reconnection, new features — without separate implementation
It restricts agents to only audio interactions for simplicity
It allows agents to bypass the SFU for lower latency
It makes agents faster at processing audio
explanation: When agents are participants, they use the same SDK and protocol as every other entity in the system. This means they automatically get NAT traversal, DTLS encryption, simulcast, multi-region routing, reconnection handling, and every new feature the platform adds. A separate agent system would require reimplementing each capability independently — years of engineering that agents get for free as participants.

question: How does the participant model make multi-agent scenarios possible?
options: Adding another agent is simply adding another participant to the room — the SFU's publish/subscribe model handles routing automatically
It requires a special orchestration layer to coordinate multiple agents
Multiple agents must share a single connection to the room
Only one agent can subscribe to a user's audio track at a time
explanation: Because agents are just participants, adding a second or third agent means connecting additional participants to the room. Each agent independently subscribes to the tracks it needs. A voice agent, a transcription agent, and a sentiment analysis agent can all subscribe to the same user audio track simultaneously without interfering with each other. The SFU routes tracks based on each participant's subscription list — no orchestration code needed.
